title: Architecture Roadmaps and Transition Planning
objectives: Create realistic architecture roadmaps that balance ambition with delivery
Sequence architecture changes to deliver incremental value
Align architecture roadmaps with funding cycles and political timelines
Design transition architectures that bridge current and target states
Communicate roadmaps to different audiences with appropriate detail
whyThisMatters:
An architecture without a roadmap is a destination without a route. You know where you want to be, but you have no plan for getting there. In government, where change happens incrementally across funding cycles, political timelines, and delivery phases, the roadmap is what turns an aspirational target state into an achievable sequence of changes.

Roadmaps fail for predictable reasons. They are too ambitious — promising transformation in timescales that are physically impossible. They are too vague — describing desired end states without specifying the steps to reach them. They ignore dependencies — sequencing work without checking whether prerequisite capabilities exist. They ignore funding reality — planning multi-year programmes without acknowledging that funding is approved annually. They ignore politics — proposing changes that conflict with ministerial priorities or cross-departmental agreements.

A good architecture roadmap is honest about constraints, specific about sequence, realistic about timelines, and valuable at every intermediate state. It does not require everything to be complete before any value is delivered. It accommodates the reality that priorities change, budgets fluctuate, and teams come and go. This lesson teaches you to build roadmaps that survive contact with reality.

content.heading: What an Architecture Roadmap Is (And Is Not)
content.body:
An architecture roadmap is a time-sequenced plan showing how the technology estate will evolve from its current state to a target state through a series of planned changes. Each change delivers identifiable value and leaves the estate in a stable, usable intermediate state.

A roadmap is NOT a project plan. A project plan specifies tasks, resources, and deadlines at a granular level. A roadmap specifies architectural states and transitions at a strategic level. The roadmap says 'by the end of Q2 2027, the authentication service will be migrated to GOV.UK One Login.' The project plan says how that migration will be executed sprint by sprint.

A roadmap is NOT a target state diagram. A target state diagram shows where you want to end up. A roadmap shows the journey — the sequence of intermediate states between now and the target. The journey matters because you cannot get from here to there in a single step. You need to sequence changes so that each step is achievable, funded, and valuable.

A roadmap is NOT a commitment. Government environments change constantly. Political priorities shift, funding is reallocated, and new requirements emerge. A roadmap is a plan — the best plan given current information. It should be reviewed and updated regularly (at least quarterly) as circumstances change. A roadmap that is never updated is either fiction or irrelevant.

A good architecture roadmap has these characteristics: it starts from an honest assessment of the current state (not a simplified or idealised version), each transition delivers identifiable value (even if the target state is not yet reached), dependencies between changes are explicit, the sequence respects funding cycles and delivery capacity, and the intermediate states are stable and operable (you are never in a state where the system does not work).

content.heading: From Current State to Target State: Defining the Journey
content.body:
The roadmap bridges three architecture views: current state (what we have today), target state (what we want to have), and the transition architecture (the intermediate states we pass through on the way).

Current state must be assessed honestly. This means documenting not just what systems exist but their condition: which are healthy and well-maintained, which are accumulating debt, which are approaching end-of-support, and which are actively constraining delivery. The Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework provides a structured approach to this assessment. If your current state assessment is optimistic, your roadmap will be unrealistic.

Target state should be defined with appropriate precision. At the strategic level, the target state describes the desired architectural characteristics: cloud-native, event-driven, API-first, aligned with cross-government platforms. At the tactical level, it describes specific system changes: legacy system X replaced by modern service Y, integration pattern A replaced by pattern B. The level of precision depends on the time horizon — near-term targets (6-12 months) should be specific, far-term targets (3-5 years) can be directional.

The transition architecture is where roadmapping gets hard. You cannot jump from current to target in one move. You need intermediate states that are each: achievable within a funding period, stable enough to operate in production, valuable enough to justify the investment, and positioned to enable the next transition.

For example, if your target state is a fully decomposed microservices architecture but your current state is a monolith, the transition might be: Phase 1 — extract the authentication module as an independent service (highest value, enables GOV.UK One Login integration). Phase 2 — extract the notification module (enables GOV.UK Notify adoption). Phase 3 — extract the payment processing (enables GOV.UK Pay integration). Each phase delivers value independently and leaves the system in a workable state, even if subsequent phases are delayed or descoped.

content.heading: Sequencing for Value, Risk, and Dependency
content.body:
The sequence in which you execute roadmap items determines whether you deliver value early or only at the end, and whether you manage risk progressively or accumulate it.

Value-first sequencing means doing the changes that deliver the most benefit earliest. This builds confidence with stakeholders (they see return on investment quickly), creates momentum for continued funding, and ensures that if the roadmap is interrupted (funding cut, priorities change), you have already delivered the most important improvements.

Risk-first sequencing means addressing the highest-risk items earliest. If a system is on end-of-support infrastructure that could fail at any time, migrating it takes priority over optimisation work on stable systems. If a critical integration has a single point of failure, adding resilience takes priority over new features. Risk-first sequencing prevents the scenario where you are still planning improvements when an avoidable failure occurs.

Dependency-aware sequencing ensures you do not plan work that depends on something that has not been done yet. If service B cannot be modernised until service A provides a modern API, then A must come before B on the roadmap. Dependency mapping is essential — and dependencies often cross team and departmental boundaries, which makes them harder to manage.

In practice, you balance all three. A useful approach: categorise roadmap items into quadrants based on value (high/low) and urgency (high/low). High value, high urgency items go first. High value, low urgency items go second. Low value, high urgency items (often risk-driven) go in parallel. Low value, low urgency items go last or are removed.

The Roadmap for Modern Digital Government (published January 2026) provides a cross-government strategic context for departmental roadmaps. Your architecture roadmap should align with the commitments and direction set out in this document — particularly where your department has specific commitments (e.g., adopting GOV.UK One Login, contributing to shared platforms, or addressing legacy systems flagged in the State of Digital Government Review).

content.heading: Aligning with Government Funding and Planning Cycles
content.body:
Government funding operates in cycles that architecture roadmaps must accommodate.

Spending Reviews set departmental budgets for multi-year periods (typically 3-4 years). Major architecture programmes should align with Spending Review bids — if your roadmap requires sustained investment over three years, the case needs to be made at Spending Review time. The Spending Review 2027 planning cycle is already beginning, and the Digital Assurance Playbook expects departmental pipelines to reflect planned commitments.

Annual Business Planning allocates the Spending Review settlement to specific programmes and activities within each year. Architecture roadmap phases should align with annual planning cycles — each year's work should be a complete, fundable package that delivers value within that year even if subsequent years are not funded.

Quarterly planning within agile delivery further decomposes annual plans into deliverable increments. Architecture roadmap milestones should be achievable within quarters so that progress is visible and demonstrable at governance checkpoints.

The practical implication: design your roadmap so that each phase is independently fundable and delivers standalone value. If Phase 2 only makes sense after Phase 3 is complete, you have created a dependency that funding cycles may break. If Phase 1 delivers value regardless of whether Phase 2 ever happens, your roadmap is resilient to funding uncertainty.

A common trap: planning a three-year roadmap with all the value at the end. Year 1 is 'foundation' work (infrastructure, platforms, technical enabling). Year 2 is 'build' (developing new capabilities). Year 3 is 'value realisation' (users actually benefit). This structure is fragile — if funding is cut after Year 1, you have spent money on foundations that deliver no value alone. Better: ensure each year delivers user-visible value, even if it is incremental.

content.heading: Communicating Roadmaps to Different Audiences
content.body:
A single roadmap needs to be presented differently to different audiences. The content is the same; the level of detail and framing changes.

For senior leadership (SRO, Director General, CTO): a one-page visual roadmap showing major transitions over time, key milestones, strategic alignment, and investment profile. They need to see: what will be different in 12 months, what it costs, what value it delivers, and what risks it addresses. Use swimlanes for parallel workstreams and colour-coding for status (planned, in progress, complete). Avoid technical detail.

For programme boards: a more detailed roadmap showing dependencies between workstreams, resource requirements, and decision points. They need to see: what decisions they need to make and when, what risks need escalation, where the roadmap depends on external factors (other departments, vendors, policy decisions), and whether progress is on track.

For delivery teams: detailed near-term roadmap items decomposed into deliverable pieces. They need to see: what they are working on this quarter, what comes next, what dependencies affect their work, and how their work fits into the bigger picture. Far-term roadmap items can be shown at lower detail.

For cross-government audiences (Enterprise Architecture team, TDC): a roadmap focused on interoperability and platform adoption. They need to see: when your department will adopt shared platforms (GOV.UK One Login, etc.), when you will expose APIs for cross-government consumption, and where your roadmap might conflict with or benefit from cross-government direction.

The cadence of communication matters. Update senior leadership quarterly. Update programme boards monthly. Update delivery teams continuously (roadmap changes are part of regular planning). Update cross-government audiences at each significant milestone.

content.heading: Transition Architectures: Living in the In-Between
content.body:
During any architecture transition, you operate a hybrid — part legacy, part modern. This hybrid state is the transition architecture, and it needs to be designed as carefully as the target state.

Transition architectures are inherently more complex than either the current or target state because they must support both old and new approaches simultaneously. Data may need to be synchronised between legacy and modern stores. Users may access some functions through the old interface and others through the new. Integrations may need to work with both old protocols and new APIs.

Design principles for transition architectures:

Minimise dual-running duration. Every day you operate both old and new systems costs money and creates risk. Plan transitions to minimise the overlap period. If you are migrating users from one system to another, migrate them in cohorts rather than running both systems indefinitely.

Make the transition invisible to users. Users should not need to know whether their request is being handled by the legacy system or the modern one. Use routing layers (API gateways, reverse proxies) to direct traffic transparently. This enables gradual migration without forcing all users to switch simultaneously.

Design for rollback. Every transition should be reversible. If the modern system develops problems, you must be able to route traffic back to the legacy system. This means keeping the legacy system operational (not decommissioned) until the modern system has proven stable in production for a defined period.

Manage data consistency. During transition, data may be modified in either the legacy or modern system. You need a strategy for keeping them consistent — typically event-driven synchronisation where changes in either system are propagated to the other. Accept that perfect consistency may not be achievable during transition; define what inconsistency is tolerable.

Document the transition state. The transition architecture is temporary but it is the state you are operating in right now. Document it clearly so the operations team knows how things work today, not just how they will work in the future. Update documentation as each transition completes.

workedExample.title: Three-Year Architecture Roadmap for DESNZ Digital Estate
workedExample.context: DESNZ operates 14 digital services across a technology estate that includes: a legacy .NET Framework platform hosting 6 services, a modern containerised platform hosting 5 services, and 3 standalone services with independent infrastructure. The Legacy IT Risk Assessment has flagged the .NET Framework platform as high-risk (framework approaching end-of-support, Windows Server 2019 approaching extended support end). The department's digital strategy commits to GOV.UK One Login adoption, GOV.UK Notify standardisation, and alignment with the Roadmap for Modern Digital Government. Budget: approximately £3 million per year for platform work plus individual service budgets.
workedExample.approach:
The Lead Solution Architect develops a three-year roadmap aligned with annual funding cycles.

Year 1 (2026-27) — Stabilise and Enable:
Q1-Q2: Migrate the .NET Framework platform to .NET 8 on containers (addresses end-of-support risk, enables future modernisation). This is risk-first sequencing — the framework end-of-support is the most urgent threat.
Q3-Q4: Implement GOV.UK One Login for the two highest-traffic citizen-facing services (delivers user value — citizens have a single login). Standardise on GOV.UK Notify for all user communications (replaces 3 different notification approaches).
Value delivered in Year 1: security risk eliminated, two services on One Login, consistent notification experience.

Year 2 (2027-28) — Consolidate and Integrate:
Q1-Q2: Migrate the 3 standalone services onto the containerised platform (reduces operational overhead — one platform to maintain instead of four). Implement shared observability stack across all services.
Q3-Q4: Roll out GOV.UK One Login to remaining citizen-facing services. Begin publishing APIs for cross-government consumption per TDC standards. Implement event-driven integration between services to replace point-to-point connections.
Value delivered in Year 2: reduced operational complexity, complete One Login adoption, first APIs for cross-government use.

Year 3 (2028-29) — Optimise and Innovate:
Q1-Q2: Decommission the .NET Framework platform entirely (all services now on modern containerised platform). Implement cross-government data sharing capabilities aligned with TDC architecture decisions.
Q3-Q4: Capacity freed from platform maintenance redirected to new service development. Evaluate emerging technologies (AI, advanced analytics) for appropriate adoption.
Value delivered in Year 3: single modern platform, cross-government interoperability, capacity for innovation.

Each year is independently valuable and fundable. If Year 3 funding is cut, Years 1 and 2 still deliver significant improvement.
workedExample.outcome: The programme board approves the roadmap with the condition that it is reviewed quarterly and updated as priorities change. The first quarterly review (after Year 1 Q1) reveals that the .NET migration is taking longer than planned due to dependency on a vendor contract negotiation. The roadmap is adjusted: GOV.UK One Login work is pulled forward into Q2 (it does not depend on the migration), and the migration completion is pushed to Q3. This flexibility — adjusting sequence without abandoning the plan — is the mark of a good roadmap.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The key design decisions were: making each year independently valuable (not front-loading all 'foundation' work), sequencing risk-first (addressing end-of-support before optimisation), and building flexibility into the plan (items that can be resequenced without breaking dependencies). The quarterly review and adjustment demonstrated that the roadmap is a living plan, not a fixed commitment — which builds trust with the programme board.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Roadmap That Survived a Machinery of Government Change
civilServiceScenario.background: Your department had a well-defined three-year architecture roadmap, funded and approved. Eighteen months in, a machinery of government change merges your department with parts of two other departments. The merged department has three separate technology estates, three different architecture teams, and three different roadmaps. Some planned work is now duplicative (two departments were independently building similar platforms). Some planned work is now impossible (shared services that assumed a single departmental identity). The new Permanent Secretary wants a unified technology strategy within 6 months.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must create a unified architecture roadmap for the merged department that: preserves the value of work already completed, eliminates duplication, addresses the most critical risks across all three estates, and delivers early visible value to demonstrate that the merger is producing better outcomes.
constraints: Three separate technology estates with different maturity levels
Existing commitments and contracts that cannot be easily unwound
Staff uncertainty — people need to see a coherent plan quickly
Budget is the sum of the three previous budgets but efficiency savings are expected
Some legacy systems from the smaller departments are in worse condition than previously known
Cross-government commitments (GOV.UK One Login adoption timelines) still apply to the merged entity
The new CTO wants cloud consolidation across all three estates within 2 years
Political pressure to show the merger delivering benefits quickly
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are appointed as the Lead Solution Architect for the merged department's architecture roadmap.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
Machinery of government changes are one of the most disruptive events for architecture roadmaps. The temptation is to start from scratch — but this wastes the investment in existing work and demoralises teams who have been delivering against the previous plan. The pragmatic approach is: assess all three estates quickly (use the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework), identify where existing roadmaps can continue unchanged (work that is specific to one part of the merged department), identify where duplication creates a choice (pick the better platform and consolidate), and identify new opportunities that the merger enables (shared platforms that serve the whole department).

The unified roadmap should have a near-term section (6 months) focused on quick wins and risk reduction, a medium-term section (12-18 months) focused on consolidation, and a longer-term section (2-3 years) focused on the target architecture for the merged department. The Permanent Secretary needs to see the near-term plan immediately — the longer-term vision can develop over the following months as understanding deepens.

practiceArtefact.description: Create a two-year architecture roadmap for a medium-sized government department transitioning from a legacy on-premises estate to cloud-native services. The current state includes: 8 services on a legacy virtualisation platform (end-of-support in 14 months), 3 services already on cloud, 2 services operated by vendors under expiring contracts, and a shared Oracle database used by 5 services. Budget is £2.5 million per year. Produce the roadmap as a structured text document.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Sequence for risk, value, and dependency. The virtualisation platform end-of-support is a hard deadline. The Oracle database creates coupling that affects sequencing. The vendor contracts create decision points. Ensure each quarter delivers identifiable value. Show dependencies between workstreams clearly.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Architecture Roadmap: Cloud Transformation Programme**

Period: Q1 2027 — Q4 2028 | Budget: £2.5M/year | Owner: Lead Solution Architect

**Current State:** 8 services on legacy virtualisation (end-of-support Nov 2027), 3 on cloud, 2 vendor-operated, shared Oracle DB coupling 5 services.

**Target State:** All services cloud-native, Oracle replaced with service-owned databases, vendor-operated services either in-sourced or re-contracted with exit provisions.

---

**Year 1: 2027 — Migrate and Decouple**

Q1 2027 (£600K):
- Migrate 3 simplest legacy services to cloud (lift-and-shift to containers — addresses end-of-support, low risk)
- Begin Oracle decoupling: extract Service A's data to its own PostgreSQL database (Service A has simplest data model)
- Decision point: vendor contract 1 expires Q2 — prepare re-procurement or in-sourcing decision

Q2 2027 (£650K):
- Migrate 2 more legacy services to cloud (these depend on Service A's Oracle data — now decoupled)
- Execute vendor contract 1 decision (re-procure through DOS7 with exit provisions, or in-source)
- Extract Service B and Service C data from Oracle (these two are tightly coupled — migrate together)

Q3 2027 (£650K):
- Migrate remaining 3 legacy services to cloud (more complex, but deadline now 2 months away)
- Continue Oracle decoupling: Service D extraction
- Decision point: vendor contract 2 expires Q4 — prepare decision

Q4 2027 (£600K):
- Decommission legacy virtualisation platform (all services migrated — deadline met)
- Execute vendor contract 2 decision
- Extract final service (Service E) from Oracle
- Decommission shared Oracle database (all services now have own databases)

Value delivered Year 1: End-of-support risk eliminated, Oracle coupling removed (enabling independent service deployment), vendor relationships restructured with exit provisions.

---

**Year 2: 2028 — Modernise and Optimise**

Q1 2028 (£600K):
- Refactor 3 highest-traffic services from lift-and-shift containers to cloud-native architecture
- Implement shared observability and monitoring across all services
- Adopt GOV.UK One Login for first citizen-facing service

Q2 2028 (£650K):
- Roll out GOV.UK One Login to remaining citizen-facing services
- Implement event-driven integration between services (replacing batch file transfers)
- Publish first APIs following GDS standards for cross-government consumption

Q3-Q4 2028 (£1.2M):
- Refactor remaining services for cloud-native patterns where justified
- Implement automated scaling and zero-downtime deployment across the estate
- Achieve full operational maturity: complete monitoring, automated DR testing, runbook coverage

Value delivered Year 2: Modern, scalable architecture, cross-government interoperability, operational excellence.

---

**Dependencies:**
- Oracle decoupling must complete before legacy platform decommission (Services on legacy depend on Oracle)
- Service A decoupling must precede Services B/C (they reference Service A's data)
- GOV.UK One Login adoption depends on cloud migration completing first (One Login libraries require modern runtime)

**Key Risks:**
1. Oracle decoupling discovers undocumented data dependencies — mitigated by discovery phase in Q1
2. Legacy migration timeline is tight for complex services — mitigated by starting with simplest
3. Vendor transitions may create service gaps — mitigated by parallel running during transition

reflectiveQuestions: Look at your department's current architecture roadmap (if one exists). Does each phase deliver value independently, or does all the value arrive at the end?
How often is your architecture roadmap reviewed and updated? If it is more than 6 months since the last update, what has changed that the roadmap does not reflect?
Have you experienced a situation where a roadmap was interrupted by a change in funding, priorities, or organisational structure? How did you adapt?
How do you communicate your roadmap to non-technical stakeholders? Do they understand what value each phase delivers and why the sequence matters?
Think about a transition architecture you have operated. What was the hardest aspect — the technical dual-running, the data consistency, or explaining to users why two systems existed simultaneously?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most important characteristic of a good architecture roadmap in government?
options: It contains the maximum detail possible about every planned change
Each phase delivers identifiable value independently, even if subsequent phases are not funded
It commits to a fixed timeline that cannot be changed
It describes only the final target state without intermediate steps
knowledgeCheck.explanation: In government, funding is approved annually and priorities change frequently. A roadmap where each phase delivers standalone value is resilient to funding cuts and priority changes. If Phase 2 is cancelled, Phase 1's value is not lost. This is the most important design principle for government roadmaps.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should you do first when creating an architecture roadmap?
options: Define the target state in maximum detail
Honestly assess the current state including system condition, risks, and constraints
Estimate the total cost of the transformation
Get approval from senior leadership for the vision
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A roadmap bridges current and target states. If the current state assessment is inaccurate or optimistic, the roadmap will be unrealistic. An honest assessment — using tools like the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework — reveals the true starting point and the most urgent risks that should be sequenced first.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should architecture roadmap phases be sequenced?
options: Always cheapest items first to show budget efficiency
Always newest technology first to demonstrate innovation
Balancing value delivery, risk reduction, and dependency order
Always in alphabetical order by system name for simplicity
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Effective sequencing balances three factors: value (do high-value items early to build confidence and justify continued investment), risk (address urgent risks like end-of-support deadlines early), and dependencies (ensure prerequisite work is complete before dependent work begins).

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a transition architecture?
options: A temporary architecture that exists only in documentation
The intermediate state between current and target where both old and new systems coexist
A simplified version of the target architecture used for testing
An architecture designed to be replaced within 6 months
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A transition architecture is the designed intermediate state where legacy and modern components coexist. It requires careful design for data consistency, user routing, and operational management. It is temporary but must be stable enough to operate in production.

knowledgeCheck.question: How often should an architecture roadmap be reviewed in government?
options: Once when it is created, then left unchanged
Only when a major incident occurs
At least quarterly, with updates when circumstances change
Annually at Spending Review time
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Government priorities, funding, and organisational structures change frequently. A roadmap must be reviewed at least quarterly and updated when significant changes occur — new priorities, funding adjustments, machinery of government changes, or new risks emerging. An outdated roadmap is worse than no roadmap because it creates false confidence.
